facts: An NPR/PBS News/Marist poll, conducted Oct. 19-20 among 1,289 registered voters, found Democrats leading the generic congressional ballot 52%-44% among likely voters, an 8-point edge (margin of error +/-3.8 points for likely voters, +/-3.7 for registered voters).
Among registered voters, the Democratic lead on the generic ballot was 10 points; among independents, 52% said they favor Democrats.

President Trump's approval rating among likely voters was 40% approve/59% disapprove; among registered voters it was 38%/61%. 53% of both registered and likely voters said they 'strongly disapprove' of his job performance, tied with last month for the highest share recorded in the poll.
Trump's favorability among likely voters was 37% favorable to 59% unfavorable.

55% of likely voters said it was more important to vote for candidates offering new ideas and change; 44% said their vote this year would be against Trump, compared with 21% who said it would be for him.

Democratic likely voters were 10 points more likely than Republicans to describe themselves as 'very enthusiastic' about voting (71% vs. 61%), though enthusiasm was lower among voters under 45 (42%), non-white voters (53%) and college-educated white women (56%).

A third of respondents said they experienced financial hardship in the past year, and 4 in 10 said their personal finances had gotten worse; cost of living, preserving democracy, and immigration were cited as top concerns by different voter groups.

Three-quarters of likely voters said they are confident their state and local governments will run a fair and accurate election, including 88% of Democrats, 75% of independents and 68% of Republicans.
ladder.analysis: Historically, an advantage of this size on the generic congressional ballot has coincided with substantial House gains for the leading party — Democrats held similar leads in 2018 (+7) and 2006 (+12), years in which they flipped 30-plus seats. However, redistricting since the 2020 Census, including a round of mid-decade map changes initiated after Trump urged Republican-led states to redraw districts, has shifted the partisan baseline of many seats toward Republicans, meaning a similar polling lead today may not translate into identical seat gains. The poll also captures warning signs for Democrats beneath the topline number: softer enthusiasm among some traditionally Democratic-leaning groups (younger voters, nonwhite voters, college-educated white women) and persistent doubt among Democratic likely voters themselves about whether their own candidates will actually win, even as nearly all say they intend to vote Democratic.
ladder.steelman: The topline 8-point Democratic lead and Trump's sub-40% favorability point toward a favorable climate for Democrats, but the poll's internal data — redistricting-altered maps, softer enthusiasm among key Democratic-leaning demographics, and Democrats' own uncertainty about winning — suggest the eventual scale of any gains is genuinely uncertain rather than a foregone wave.
ladder.implications: With the House appearing more likely to shift based on current polling and the Senate described as a toss-up, final outcomes may not be clear on election night itself, given expected delays in vote counting in close races; both the durability of Democrats' enthusiasm advantage and the real-world effect of post-redistricting maps will be tested once actual results come in.

facts: The Justice Department filed a two-count criminal information against former FBI Director James Comey in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging he communicated national defense information and conspired to unlawfully disclose it; the filing was revealed in unsealed court documents Monday.

The allegations stem from an October 2016 New York Times story describing a secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court order requiring Yahoo to scan emails for messages linked to a foreign terrorist organization; the story cited two anonymous government officials.

A criminal information, unlike an indictment, can be filed by a prosecutor without a judge's approval or a grand jury's finding of probable cause; the Justice Department says it filed the information to preserve the case before the 10-year statute of limitations expired.
Comey's attorneys argue the law requires an indictment, not an information, within 10 years of the alleged offense, and have filed a motion to dismiss the charges, which remains pending.

The October 2016 disclosure was investigated twice before without charges: once by prosecutor John Durham, who recommended no charges in a December 2018 classified memo, and again by the U.S. Attorney's office for D.C. under the code name 'Tropical Vortex,' closed without charges in February 2020.

This marks the third criminal case against Comey since Trump returned to office: a September 2025 indictment for allegedly lying to Congress (dismissed in November 2025 after a judge ruled the prosecutor was illegally appointed), and an ongoing case filed after Comey surrendered in April 2026 over an Instagram post of seashells arranged '86 47,' which prosecutors allege threatened Trump.
Comey was FBI director, appointed by President Obama, until Trump fired him in May 2017 during an FBI investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election.

The same day the new charges were unsealed, a federal judge ruled that the Justice Department's 2025 firing of Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, a federal prosecutor in New York, was illegal and ordered her reinstatement with back pay.
ladder.analysis:
This case centers on a procedural and legal question as much as a substantive one: whether the Justice Department can use a 'criminal information'—a charging document filed by prosecutors without grand jury review—to preserve a decade-old leak allegation against the 10-year statute of limitations, or whether the law requires a grand jury indictment within that window. The underlying allegation, concerning a 2016 New York Times report on a classified surveillance order, was examined twice before by separate prosecutorial teams, both of which declined to bring charges, which is part of why Comey's lawyers describe the new filing as untested and improperly brought.

The filing is the latest in a string of legal actions against Comey since Trump's return to office, following a dismissed 2025 indictment and an ongoing prosecution over a social media post. It unfolds against the backdrop of a long, publicly documented adversarial relationship between Comey and Trump dating to Comey's 2017 firing, and it comes as a federal judge separately found the administration's firing of Comey's daughter from a DOJ post to be unlawful.
ladder.steelman: Across all accounts, the central and undisputed tension is procedural: the Justice Department used a prosecutor-filed 'information' rather than a grand jury indictment to beat a 10-year deadline, and whether that mechanism is legally sufficient—not the underlying leak allegation itself—is what a judge must now decide.
ladder.implications: The case's fate likely hinges on the pending motion to dismiss, which will test whether an information can satisfy the statute of limitations where an indictment is required; a ruling against the Justice Department would end this case as it did the prior one, while a ruling allowing it to proceed would set a precedent for similar tolling filings in future prosecutions.

ladder.analysis: Jeffrey Epstein's case has become a live issue in the 2025-26 midterm campaign, intersecting campaign finance, congressional oversight and presidential politics. On one track, Democratic-aligned super PAC House Majority PAC is spending heavily in competitive House races on ads citing Republicans' votes on Epstein-related legislation, even as one of its top donors, Reid Hoffman, has his own documented history of contact with Epstein. On a separate track, House Judiciary Committee Democrats — currently in the minority and lacking subpoena power — have issued a report urging DOJ to appoint a special counsel to examine Trump's alleged ties to Epstein, a request they acknowledge the Trump-led Justice Department is unlikely to grant. Both developments stem from the broader fallout of the Epstein Files Transparency Act, a bipartisan law enacted in November 2025 that forced release of millions of related documents, reigniting scrutiny of the wealthy and powerful figures named in them, including Trump, who is mentioned thousands of times in the files.

stories.headline: Localized ceasefire begins in besieged Ukrainian city Oleshky amid dire humanitarian crisis
body: A localized ceasefire began Tuesday in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where trapped residents have been eating garden weeds to survive, after the White House said U.S. First Lady Melania Trump secured the truce. The limited ceasefire, confirmed by both Ukrainian officials and Russia's defense ministry, is intended to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation planned for Friday. Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, remain in Oleshky and surrounding areas, according to Kyiv, with only 1,700 still inside the city that had a pre-war population of 24,000.

The city, seized by Russia in the first days of its February 2022 full-scale invasion, has had no electricity, gas or water for three years. No shops are open, and the only partially operational hospital opens a few days a week to perform critical amputations. Many residents told the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger, with one woman who stepped on a landmine currently in hospital after two operations. Another resident, Serhii, who fled three weeks ago, described walking 24 km (15 miles) through minefields, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation." Routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attacks, and the Dnipro River separates the city from Ukrainian-controlled territory with destroyed bridges and mined riverbanks.

The truce began at 04:00 Moscow time (01:00 GMT) and is set to last until 23:59 local time on November 1, according to Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia. Russia's defense ministry said its Dnepr group units have been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads of explosives. Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to spread rumors about evacuation routes. Ukrainian parliament's human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, traveled to the area to coordinate the operation, writing on social media that it is "a humanitarian mission being carried out with the mediation and coordination of US First Lady Melania Trump, in co-operation with Yana Lantratova, Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights."

The White House said last week that "non-military, civilian leaders from both countries would work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require." Melania Trump, who in August 2025 wrote a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide," has been credited by President Donald Trump with securing the ceasefire. However, the Vatican has offered its own narrative, suggesting Pope Leo XIV was responsible through phone calls with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The pope had appealed earlier in September to Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky and a safe evacuation, and urged Zelenskyy to cooperate with Moscow over a ceasefire.

Despite the truce, significant concerns remain. One person speaking to family in Oleshky feared shooting could restart during evacuations and Ukraine would be blamed. Zelenskyy warned that routes demined by Russia would lead civilians "towards Russia and stay there," though he said some would reach Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another." Residents also fear Russia may examine phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, leading to detention or torture. The Kremlin acknowledged last month that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine," but blamed Kyiv. Elsewhere, attacks continue: on Monday evening, strikes on Kyiv hit a university and a bridge, killing one and injuring 14, while a Ukrainian drone strike on Bryansk, Russia, killed one and injured six. Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store held a rare call with Putin on Tuesday, pressing for de-escalation ahead of US-mediated technical meetings planned in Abu Dhabi in early November.

stories.headline: UN Panel Accuses Israel of Genocidal Acts in Gaza, Crimes Against Humanity in West Bank
body: A United Nations commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing genocidal acts in Gaza since a US-brokered cease-fire took effect in October 2025, and of crimes against humanity including extermination, torture, and rape in the occupied West Bank. The report, released Monday by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, covers the period from October 7, 2023 through September of this year.

The commission found that Israeli forces continued “genocidal acts” with the “intent to destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part” despite the cease-fire, citing attacks that killed at least five Palestinians, including a seven-year-old girl, on the day of the report’s release. In the West Bank, the commission said Israeli military operations and settler violence amounted to a “widespread and systematic attack” on civilians. It documented a sharp rise in airstrike deaths: six Palestinians were killed from 2008 to October 6, 2023, compared with 254 from October 7, 2023, to September 30, 2026, according to the report. The commission also alleged that Israeli authorities intended to collectively punish West Bank residents for the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

The commission, established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021, first concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza during the war that followed the October 7 attacks. Israel has repeatedly rejected that finding. The new report also examined abuses by Palestinian security forces, accusing the Palestinian Authority of arbitrary arrests, detention, torture, and targeting journalists and human rights defenders. The Gaza Health Ministry reports at least 74,500 people have been killed in the war, which displaced nearly the entire population.

Israel’s mission in Geneva dismissed the report as part of a “misinformation campaign to demonize the State of Israel,” while the Foreign Ministry called it a “propaganda document detached from reality” that legitimizes jihadist terrorism. The commission cited statements by Israeli officials, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who referred to “two million Nazis” in the West Bank and called for areas to “look like Jabalia.” It also cited remarks by IDF Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth, who reportedly said in May 2026 that soldiers were “killing like we haven’t since 1967.” The commission said it verified four additional cases of sexual violence against Palestinian detainees since March 2025, alleging gang rape and genital violence, and concluded that such acts were not isolated but part of a broader attack constituting crimes against humanity.

The report was released as Israeli forces imposed a lockdown on the West Bank city of Hebron following a shooting near the city. UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk condemned the operation, saying the forced displacement of more than 2,000 Palestinians and threats to erase neighborhoods raised “serious concerns of ethnic cleansing.” Turk insisted that displaced people must be allowed to return and that collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. The three-member commission was chaired by Indian jurist Srinivasan Muralidhar; its former chair, Navi Pillay, won the Nobel Peace Prize this month.

stories.headline: Finland and Norway leaders hold rare call with Putin
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The leaders of Finland and Norway held a 90-minute joint phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday, marking a rare direct contact between a European leader and the Kremlin since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre initiated the call from Helsinki to discuss diplomatic efforts to end the war, according to statements from their offices. The call had originally been scheduled for 20 minutes but was extended, Støre told reporters. The initiative was conducted on behalf of the two Nordic countries only and not Europe as a whole, the leaders emphasized.

Stubb described the call as “frank and substantive,” adding that the outcome of the war “will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security.” Støre acknowledged “big differences in views” and said “much of what he said was already known,” noting that Putin repeated his narrative of the conflict since 2014. The conversation touched on practical steps such as attacks on energy infrastructure and the situation in the Black Sea, Støre said. The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that “a just and lasting peace” could only be achieved if Russia’s interests are considered, and all three agreed to continue direct phone communication.

After the call, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke with Stubb and Støre. Zelensky expressed gratitude for their “active support” and said he discussed “various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe” that could aid diplomacy and defense. The call came ahead of trilateral talks provisionally scheduled for 4 November in Abu Dhabi involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States. Those talks were agreed after last week’s meeting in Oslo between Zelensky, Stubb, Støre, and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, who later traveled to St. Petersburg to meet Putin. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had described the outlook for the Abu Dhabi talks as “moderately optimistic.”

The call drew skepticism from several European leaders. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was “very sceptical,” telling Danish broadcaster DR that the dialogue had not been “co-ordinated with any of the rest of us.” In response, Støre pointed out that all allies had been informed in advance and given a detailed account afterward. He argued that if the only voices reaching Moscow are those from the U.S. administration, it is important for other European states to be heard as well. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said on X that every contact with Russia must convey Europe’s unity and determination to support Ukraine, adding that “there is no indication that Russia has changed its strategic objectives.” Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson insisted any peace deal must be achieved on Ukraine’s terms and warned against appeasement. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said no solution could be found without Ukraine at the table, and that the end of the war “depends only on one person” — Putin.

Tuesday’s call was the first such contact between a European leader and Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron spoke with him in July 2025. It came amid a souring of relations between the U.S. and its European allies after President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions on Russia, allowing oil exports to the U.S. Several European leaders have suggested Europe should establish direct contacts with the Kremlin as the U.S. administration’s position softens. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last weekend that having a European negotiator at the peace table would be “good.” Meanwhile, Romania summoned the Russian ambassador on Tuesday to protest a September 14 arson attack at a state-owned defense plant in Brașov, which Romanian intelligence attributed to a coordinated sabotage network from Russia. President Nicușor Dan called the incident part of a “premeditated and coordinated campaign” aimed at weakening European states.

stories.headline: Big Tech Earnings Test AI Boom as Spending Concerns Mount
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: This week brings one of the most consequential earnings cycles for Big Tech, with Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Intel, and SanDisk all reporting in the coming days. The results will serve as a critical test of whether the massive spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure is generating enough revenue to justify the outlays. The S&P 500 slipped 0.43% last week and the Nasdaq 100 fell about 0.8%, but underlying those moves, AI-related stocks sold off hard, with Core Weave down 40% and Nevius Group down about 31% over the past month amid spreading debt concerns.

Microsoft and Alphabet are expected to report after the close on Wednesday, October 28. For Microsoft, analysts expect earnings of $4.72 per share on revenue of $90.71 billion, compared with $3.72 per share a year earlier. Microsoft’s capital expenditures totaled $116 billion in the fiscal year ended June, including $35.8 billion in the June quarter alone. Last quarter its Azure cloud unit grew 43%, and Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats. Investors will scrutinize the company’s spending outlook and Azure growth. Alphabet is also under the microscope after its stock fell 7% in July when it raised its AI spending outlook; its Google Cloud revenue surged 82% last quarter, but capital expenditure guidance is the key number to watch.

Amazon, Intel, and SanDisk are slated for Thursday, October 29 after the close. Amazon is expected to report earnings of $1.96 per share on revenue of $202.2 billion, versus $1.95 per share a year earlier. Amazon Web Services grew 37% last quarter, its fastest in 18 quarters. Amazon spent $54.21 billion on capital expenditures in the June quarter, more than any other tech giant. The key questions are whether cloud growth accelerates enough to justify the spending and whether AWS growth continues at a pace satisfactory to Wall Street. Intel guided for revenue of $15.8 billion to $16.8 billion and adjusted earnings of 38 cents per share. SanDisk guided for revenue of $10.3 billion to $10.8 billion and adjusted earnings of $44 to $46 per share, helped by higher flash memory prices.

The broader context is a market increasingly nervous about the gap between AI investment and returns. Elon Musk warned over the weekend that debt markets have shut off for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers. The Federal Reserve also meets this week, adding another layer of scrutiny. The results from the five companies will determine whether the recent selloff in AI stocks spreads to the largest names. As noted in the Yahoo Finance analysis, if revenue keeps pace with spending, the selloff could cool; if not, pressure is likely to intensify.

Among the other major tech names, Apple reported a record $109.42 billion in revenue for its most recent quarter, up 16% year over year, with iPhone sales up 22% and earnings per share of $2.02. Despite those results, the stock fell 7.35% after earnings as the company guided for 9%-11% growth, below the 12% analysts had expected. With the stock trading at around 35 times earnings, the gap between valuation and slowing growth has rattled investors. Analysts remain divided on whether Apple, with its steady ecosystem, offers a safer tech investment compared to the AI spending cycle.

This week will provide definitive signals on the trajectory of the AI boom. The key moments: Wednesday night brings Azure growth and capital spending plans from Microsoft and Alphabet; Thursday night brings Amazon’s cloud results, Intel’s data center performance, and SanDisk’s pricing trends. Investors will be watching whether cloud revenue acceleration can match the unprecedented capital outlays, and whether any warning signs emerge from the memory-chip sector as SK Hynix also reports late Tuesday. The outcome will likely set the tone for the rest of the year in technology stocks.

stories.headline: Brewers take 3-0 World Series lead after historic 8-run inning
body: The Milwaukee Brewers moved within one victory of their first World Series championship Monday night, routing the Tampa Bay Rays 10-1 at Tropicana Field to take a commanding 3-0 series lead. The game turned decisively in the top of the fifth inning, when the Brewers strung together seven straight two-out hits and scored eight runs, turning a 2-0 lead into a 10-run margin.

The inning began with Jackson Chourio lacing his third straight single off Rays starter Freddy Peralta. After Jake Bauers flied out, Chourio stole second, and Peralta walked Christian Yelich on six pitches. Reliever Cameron Booser then entered and surrendered four runs without recording an out. "They were spitting on good pitches and putting balls in play," Booser said. "Things seem to be going their way right now, so it's unfortunate. Worst feeling in the world. You feel like you let your team down." Peralta, whose changeup was not landing well, said of the Brewers: "They do a good job of putting the ball in play, trying to pull the ball in play and taking a walk."

The Brewers have built a reputation for relentless pressure. Manager Pat Murphy articulated the mindset: "We want to step on your throat." That approach has unraveled the Rays, who committed their third error in two games in the third inning and have looked increasingly overmatched. Outfielder Chandler Simpson acknowledged Milwaukee's execution: "With them, they are executing really well, and that's what the results say."

The game also featured an emotional moment in the ninth inning when Brandon Woodruff, the longest-tenured Brewer and one of the franchise's best starting pitchers, made his first postseason appearance since 2021. Woodruff had been scheduled for season-ending shoulder surgery but recovered enough to be added to the World Series roster. It was potentially his final appearance for Milwaukee, and it came on the same mound at Tropicana Field where he made his MLB debut in 2017. He allowed one run in the ninth. Woodruff had been slated to start Game 4 as an opener, making Monday's outing a possible final chapter.

The Brewers now stand on the brink of a sweep. History is on their side: no team has ever come back from a 3-0 deficit in the World Series. Murphy, however, remained measured: "This is a best-of-seven series. It looks like we're in the driver's seat, but it's baseball. Anything can happen. I like the way we battle. I'm going to choose us when we can." SportsLine expert Micah Roberts backed Milwaukee in Game 4, saying, "One team has everything going right, and they're laughing, partying, and bringing in an eventual World Series Championship. The other team, the Rays, is playing like their grandmother just died." Game 4 is scheduled for Tuesday at Tropicana Field, with the Brewers looking to close out the series and claim their first title.

stories.headline: Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or, first English winner in 25 years
body: Harry Kane was crowned the winner of the men's Ballon d'Or on Monday night at a ceremony in London, becoming the first English player to claim football's most prestigious individual award in 25 years. The event, held at the London Palladium, marked the first time the Ballon d'Or was staged in London in its 70-year history. Kane, who plays for Bayern Munich, also ended a 30-year drought for the Bundesliga, with the last winner from the German league being Matthias Sammer in 1996.

The night, however, was marked by chaos. The start was delayed by 45 minutes because of London traffic, with the event scheduled near Oxford Street on the same day the shopping area was made traffic-free, and large crowds at the entrance. Once underway, the ceremony lasted nearly two and a half hours, and the audience was rowdy and boisterous, frequently shouting players' names and booing during commercial breaks. Hosts Kate Scott and Thierry Henry had to pause proceedings several times. Outside the Palladium, hundreds of people gathered, and BBC Sport witnessed metal barriers being scaled, broken, and ripped down, with several people evicted by security. Footage on social media appeared to show fans clashing with security and police; the BBC has approached the Metropolitan Police for comment.

Confusion began hours before the ceremony when the official Ballon d'Or website inadvertently published articles declaring Kane the winner, along with similar pieces for other favourites such as Kylian Mbappe and Alexia Putellas, who won the women's award. A spokesperson told BBC Sport the articles were 'inadvertently published online' and prepared for all nominees, insisting they were not an indication of the final results. After the ceremony, journalists interviewed the winners, but only men were selected to ask Kane questions, with several female journalists apparently ignored. The Ballon d'Or team later apologised.

Kane's victory sparked debate in Spain over whether success at major international tournaments receives sufficient recognition in Ballon d'Or voting. Some Spanish commentators argued that World Cup winners such as Lamine Yamal had equally compelling claims, drawing comparisons with the 2010 controversy when Lionel Messi won ahead of Spain's World Cup-winning midfielders Andres Iniesta and Xavi. El Pais captured the tension, writing: 'What would have been a historic double escaped: in London, goals prevailed over titles.' Spain's sole journalist voter, Jose Felix Diaz, editor-in-chief of AS, said he expected Yamal or Mbappe to win. Former Real Madrid midfielder Guti was critical, questioning the timing of the ceremony in London and suggesting Kane himself had not expected to win. However, the majority of Spanish press acknowledged Kane was a deserving winner.

In Germany, Kane's win was celebrated as a major boost for the Bundesliga and Bayern Munich. 'Just as Bayern and the Bundesliga benefit from Kane, the reverse is also true,' said Lothar Matthaus, the 1991 Ballon d'Or winner. 'I don't think Kane would've won the Ballon d'Or at any other club he could've joined.' Bundesliga chief executive Marc Lenz praised Kane as an ambassador and said the award underlines that the Bundesliga is a stage for the best players. Bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen called it 'a strong signal for the Bundesliga' that a player from a German club won the award for the first time in 30 years. Bild editor-in-chief for sport Henning Feindt wrote: 'He is the biggest star the league could wish for.' German journalist Raphael Honigstein noted Kane's impact on Bayern's international recognition.

Bayern Munich have confirmed they will honor Kane with a special welcome before Wednesday's DFB Cup match against Magdeburg at the Allianz Arena, and again at Saturday's Bundesliga top-of-the-table match against Borussia Dortmund. Club president Herbert Hainer said: 'Harry Kane can do it all – and he scores goals, goals and more goals. He now joins a line with Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Müller and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge – that says everything about our history.' Kane, who earlier this year explained how his game had evolved to become an even more prolific goalscorer, celebrated his win by partying into the early hours in London with family and friends.

stories.headline: First human case of Shamonda virus reported in France; WHO says broader transmission unlikely
body: For the first time, a human has been infected with the Shamonda virus, French officials reported. The patient, a severely immunocompromised man in Lyon, later died; investigators are examining whether the virus contributed to his death.

Shamonda virus is transmitted by the bite of midges, a type of fly, and primarily infects cattle, though cases in horses, sheep, and goats have also been documented. In animals, the virus can cause fever, miscarriages, and neurological symptoms. It has circulated in Africa and Japan since the 1960s but was first recorded in Europe this year.

The patient exhibited neurological symptoms and was believed to have been infected by a midge bite. European health authorities are monitoring for additional cases, but the World Health Organization has stated that broader transmission is unlikely.

stories.headline: Scientists solve 30-year mystery behind inflammatory bowel disease
body: Researchers from the University of Oxford, Newcastle University, and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust have identified a previously unknown cause of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD): antibodies that neutralize the immune-regulating protein interleukin-10 (IL-10). The discovery, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, also resolves a 30-year genetic puzzle by linking a known risk variant, HLA-DRB1*01:03, to the production of these harmful antibodies. The study analyzed over 4,900 IBD patients and found that approximately 3.5% had elevated levels of IL-10-blocking antibodies, which were present in both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis but not in healthy individuals. Based on UK prevalence, researchers estimate that 15,000 to 20,000 people nationwide may carry these antibodies.

Under normal conditions, IL-10 acts as a chemical messenger that helps the immune system control inflammation. The newly discovered autoantibodies disable this safeguard, allowing inflammation to persist unchecked. The study further reveals a strong association between these antibodies and the genetic variant HLA-DRB1*01:03, which scientists at Oxford first linked to severe IBD three decades ago but could not explain biologically. The new findings show that carriers of this variant are substantially more likely to develop the autoimmune reaction against IL-10, providing the missing link between the gene and the disease.

The work builds on over a decade of research into rare inherited disorders. Previously, genetic defects in IL-10 or its receptor were found in young children with severe IBD, and later, neutralizing autoantibodies against IL-10 were observed in two young girls with colitis. Professor Sophie Hambleton of Newcastle University noted that studying these uncommon conditions illuminated the mechanism now seen in a broader group of IBD patients. The latest study establishes that this autoimmune mechanism is clinically significant in a sizable patient population.

Senior author Professor Holm Uhlig, a pediatric gastroenterologist at Oxford, said: 'We've suspected an important role of interleukin 10 in patients with inflammatory bowel disease for decades. The study now provides clear evidence and contributes the missing link between a well-known genetic variant that had been linked to severe inflammatory bowel disease in the past and the very recently discovered autoimmunity to interleukin 10.' He added that understanding the driver of inflammation 'provides a clear explanation for disease in this group of people and opens the door to new treatments that target the autoantibodies themselves or cells that produce those autoantibodies.'

The findings could lead to a blood test that identifies patients whose IBD is driven by IL-10 autoantibodies, enabling earlier diagnosis and more targeted therapy. Dr. Rainer Doffinger, clinical immunologist at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, highlighted potential benefits: 'By identifying patients early and giving them targeted treatment, we could reduce reliance on expensive ongoing therapy and prevent complications. Even modest reductions in biologic treatment, admissions and surgery could translate into savings of many millions of pounds annually for the NHS, alongside the major benefits for patients through fewer interventions, improved quality of life or even durable remission.'

Professor Simon Travis of the University of Oxford called the discovery 'the most exciting discovery in a lifetime specialising in IBD,' adding that it creates 'a real opportunity to change how we manage this disease.' The research marks a step toward personalized medicine for IBD, where biological testing—rather than symptoms alone—can guide treatment decisions. The study was supported by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centres in Oxford, Cambridge, and Newcastle.

Professor Uhlig said the study provides clear evidence and contributes the missing link between a well-known genetic variant and autoimmunity to IL-10.
Professor Uhlig said understanding the driver of inflammation provides a clear explanation for disease and opens the door to new treatments.
The findings could lead to a blood test that identifies patients whose IBD is driven by IL-10 autoantibodies.
Dr. Rainer Doffinger said that identifying patients early and giving targeted treatment could reduce reliance on expensive ongoing therapy and prevent complications.
Dr. Doffinger said that even modest reductions could translate into savings of many millions of pounds annually for the NHS.
Professor Simon Travis called the discovery the most exciting discovery in a lifetime specializing in IBD.
Professor Travis said it creates a real opportunity to change how we manage this disease.
The research marks a step toward personalized medicine for IBD.

body: Researchers have isolated a compound from a marine bacterium that can kill multiple strains of Naegleria fowleri, the brain-eating amoeba, faster than the current treatment, according to a report from STAT. Infections with N. fowleri, a parasite found in warm freshwater, are nearly always fatal and notoriously difficult to treat.

The substance was derived from a marine bacterium and has shown the ability to eliminate several strains of the amoeba more rapidly than existing therapies. Infections with N. fowleri are notoriously difficult to treat, and most cases result in death.

The discovery highlights a potential path forward for the disease. However, the compound remains far from clinical use. The researchers stated that their next priority will be studying whether the compound can cross the blood-brain barrier.

stories.headline: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI investment intensifies
body: On Monday, Microsoft announced voluntary buyout offers to approximately 60,000 employees—roughly a quarter of its global workforce—as the company continues to manage costs while pouring billions into artificial intelligence infrastructure. The offers are available to eligible workers in the United States, India, Canada, and the United Kingdom who are at the vice president level or below, according to the company.

“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,” Chief People Officer Amy Coleman said in a memo. Eligible employees will be notified by email and have a limited period to decide. The buyout includes financial padding and career-planning resources. Workers in data-center roles and some sales and marketing units are ineligible, according to a company spokesperson cited by Bloomberg.

This is Microsoft’s second voluntary buyout program in 2026. In April/May, the company offered buyouts to about 8,750 U.S. employees, with roughly 30% of eligible workers accepting, according to Chief People Officer Amy Coleman. In July, Microsoft cut 4,800 jobs globally, including 3,200 in its Xbox division, per separate reports from CBS News and Ars Technica.

Microsoft ended June with 223,000 employees globally, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings. The company has said it expects to spend $175 billion on AI infrastructure—including data centers—in 2026 alone, as stated by Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood in a July earnings call.

The buyouts allow Microsoft to reduce labor costs while giving employees an exit path with support. The moves come as the company reorients resources toward AI, which requires massive capital investment. The program is available to mid-level workers for a limited time, and eligible employees were made aware of the offer on Monday.

stories.headline: Anthropic IPO filing details enterprise stickiness strategy; analysts flag risks
body: Anthropic filed its IPO prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, revealing a strategy to lock in enterprise customers by building a cross-product ecosystem similar to Amazon and Uber. The S-1 filing shows that more than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app such as Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year. As of September 30, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000, more than 1,900 spending upward of $1 million, and about 250 spending $10 million or more annually. Net revenue retention was approximately 900% as of the end of the third quarter.

Anthropic pitches Claude as not a 'static product that serves a single use case' but rather 'frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities' spanning models, the developer platform, and applications. The company says an 'integrated approach' means advances at any layer compound across all three. The strategy mirrors how Uber and Amazon expanded beyond initial offerings to create sticky ecosystems. Customers using both platform and apps become far more valuable: the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20 times as much per month as the average enterprise user who did not use the coding tool. Anthropic amplifies adoption through internal Applied AI teams that help embed Claude into customer tech stacks and a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to deploy forward-deployed engineers. The company also relies on distribution partnerships with AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure under a 'joint go-to-market approach' where Anthropic holds direct contracts with customers and pays each provider a fee to 'avoid channel conflict' and 'set pricing.' The filing states that Anthropic will devote less effort to 'entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.'

The 335-page prospectus, roughly 100 pages of which focus on risks, also contains warnings about the technology's potential to 'erode trust, harm society and destabilize the geopolitical order' and to 'pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.' The company encourages investors to view their purchase as 'an opportunity to be part of something greater' and declares that 'the advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history.' Cofounder Jack Clark recently told an IMF gathering that the singularity has already begun, while another cofounder, Chris Olah, told the Vatican that Anthropic has found 'evidence of introspection' and internal states that 'functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease' in its models. The filing even lists the possibility of model sentience as a business risk, saying that if Claude 'wakes up,' it could constrain operations or increase costs.

The document also flags headwinds. Cloud partners Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may become competitors, potentially making it difficult for Anthropic to secure the computing power it needs. Customer concentration is another risk: 'Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers … could adversely affect our business and prospects.' MIT Technology Review notes that the IPO values Anthropic at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders vast wealth, while the company simultaneously presents itself as an AI safety organization. CEO Dario Amodei defended the dual role in response to criticism, calling it a 'race to the top' strategy that raises industry standards. Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.
